content:
Jakub Pachocki, the CSO of OpenAI published this essay yesterday. While the focus of the essay is Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) of AI models, he said something interesting about mathematics research. Apparently this isn't something they are actively prioritising:

For instance, we believe we could make the models better at specifically mathematics research with additional focus, but we do not prioritize this direction because of the urgency we feel about RSI and automated alignment research, as I will discuss later.

I don't have any insight beyond what's in the article, but I thought it was interesting -- maybe this is part of the reason why the FLT result came out of a lab associated with Anthropic?

To me, what he's saying sounds like "they don't build special purpose models for math". They are probably still throwing their general purpose models at some math problems hoping for some good results and the PR that comes with it.

Well, this didn't age well! Apparently they just solved a Millenium Prize problem...

https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/

Solving a Millennium Prize problem is not inconsistent with not prioritizing making models specifically better at math. It could be that the model just turns out to be good enough to solve a Millennium Prize problem even with no special attempt to train it to be better at math.
It was another internal model. Maybe it is the "gpt-6-aeon" that appears on codex strings but hasn´t been released

It is naïve to think OpenAI is not training their models specifically at mathematics. Almost surely they are, while claiming they are not, to imply "our models are just that good" to increase the hype value. Bear in mind OpenAI is an unprofitable company that exists exclusively because of hype bringing investor's money.
Could someone summarize briefly about the drama :)))

Timothy Chow said:

Solving a Millennium Prize problem is not inconsistent with not prioritizing making models specifically better at math. It could be that the model just turns out to be good enough to solve a Millennium Prize problem even with no special attempt to train it to be better at math.

If the model is good enough to do Navier Stokes, I think it is the endgame to the traditional mathematical research. Although there are infinitely many mathematical problems and there are many harder than Navier Stokes, but with that speed of development, I think eventually in the not far future, new mathematical research will come from AI
Haha and seems like the statement that they will cure all dieseses in 10 years is now make some sense
But it is still very very hard
